A.explanation: This uses $\frac{1}{2}m(\Delta v)^2/t$ with $\Delta v = 5\text{ m s}^{-1}$, giving about $4.2\text{ kW}$. Kinetic energy depends on $v^2$, so use $v^2-u^2$, not $(v-u)^2$.

B.explanation: The gain in kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}m(v^2-u^2) = 202500\text{ J}$ divided by $5.4\text{ s}$ gives about $37500\text{ W}$, which is $38\text{ kW}$.

C.explanation: This is about three times larger than $\Delta E_k/t$ for $20\text{ m s}^{-1}$ to $25\text{ m s}^{-1}$. It does not equal the actual kinetic energy gain divided by $5.4\text{ s}$.

D.explanation: This is about $1100\text{ kW}$, almost 30 times the useful power from the kinetic energy change. It is far too large for a $1800\text{ kg}$ car gaining $5\text{ m s}^{-1}$ in $5.4\text{ s}$.

hints: Notice the road is horizontal, so the useful work becomes extra kinetic energy as speed rises from $20\text{ m s}^{-1}$ to $25\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Recall that change in kinetic energy is $\frac{1}{2}m(v^2-u^2)$, not $\frac{1}{2}m(v-u)^2$, with $m = 1800\text{ kg}$.
Divide that energy gain in $\text{J}$ by the time $5.4\text{ s}$ to get average power in $\text{W}$, then express the result in $\text{kW}$ for comparison with the options.
walkthrough: Identify the useful energy transfer: on a horizontal road the engine increases kinetic energy from $u = 20\text{ m s}^{-1}$ to $v = 25\text{ m s}^{-1}$ for $m = 1800\text{ kg}$.
State the governing relations: $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ and average useful power $P = \Delta E_k/t$ with $t = 5.4\text{ s}$.
This gives $\Delta E_k = 900 \times 225 = 202500\text{ J}$ of useful work done by the engine.
Divide by time: $P = 202500/5.4 \approx 37500\text{ W}$, and check units of $\text{J s}^{-1} = \text{W}$.
Convert to kilowatts: $37500\text{ W} = 37.5\text{ kW}$, about $38\text{ kW}$. This is option B.
